title: The forgiveness of sins
hookLine: metanoia means a change of mind, a turning around

cards: You're driving somewhere new. The map app says turn left; you're sure it's right. You turn right.

Ten minutes later the road narrows, the houses thin out, and a sinking feeling arrives: you're going the wrong way. Keep going, pride intact, hoping the road bends back. Or pull over, admit it, and turn around.
That moment isn't dramatic. Nobody claps. But everything after it is different.
The creed says, I believe in the forgiveness of sins, and the New Testament word for the way there is today's word. It carries a lot of baggage. Underneath, it's about turning the car around.

teach.b: In English, repentance sounds heavy: sackcloth, guilt, someone shouting on a street corner. But the Greek word in the New Testament is metanoia. Meta, change or beyond.
Noia, from nous, the mind. A change of mind: a new way of seeing that turns your life around.
The Hebrew prophets used a plainer word, shuv: turn, return. Ezekiel pleads: "wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye."
And the first words of Jesus in Mark's Gospel are: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel." Turn around. Something good is here.
Think of the prodigal son in the pigsty.
Luke says, "And when he came to himself," he got up and went home. That's metanoia. The father sees him a long way off and runs.
The forgiveness was waiting before he'd finished his speech.

A piece of history: the Latin Bible of the Western church rendered repent as do penance. When scholars went back to the Greek, some, including Luther, argued the word meant a change of heart, not only a set of acts.

Luther's very first thesis said Jesus meant the whole life of believers to be repentance. Catholic teaching also says the outward acts must come from an inward turning. Churches practice it differently.
Catholics and Orthodox, and some Anglicans and Lutherans, confess to a priest and hear words of forgiveness. Protestant churches often confess together in worship, or privately to God.
Each pairs the same two things: turn, and be forgiven. This week's path: the cross, the descent, the third day, the Spirit, the church, the saints, and now forgiveness.

how: Christians often confess their sins in a prayer said together at worship; Catholics, Orthodox and some Anglicans and Lutherans also go to individual confession with a priest, and Lent is a season especially set aside for repentance.

o: feeling deeply sorry and guilty for a wrong
a change of mind that turns your life around
a penalty you pay to make up for a sin

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: the Greek word for repentance is mostly about feeling guilty
metanoia means a change of mind, a turning around.
Jesus's first words in Mark include repent
in the parable, the father waits for the son to finish apologizing before he forgives
he sees him a long way off and runs to him.

games.q: you're the younger son, feeding pigs, starving, far from home. what happens next in the story?
o: you stay, too ashamed to go back.
you come to yourself, get up and go home.
you write your father a letter.
games.why: "And when he came to himself," he got up and went home. his father saw him a long way off and ran.

practice: Think of one small road you're on that's heading the wrong way: a habit, a grudge, the way you've been talking to someone. See yourself pulling over and turning the wheel, and ask what the first stretch of road back looks like.
If you pray, ask God for forgiveness and for help with the turn; if you don't, simply decide, gently, on the first step.

wordCard.voice: Repentance. From the Greek metanoia, a change of mind: turning your life around, toward God and toward home.

orig.note: Greek: a change of mind, from meta, change, and nous, mind. The New Testament word for repentance.

carryVoice: Your line: turn, and be forgiven. The father was already running. That's the week, day three hundred eight.
